newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel says reforms to cut net tax burden.
newsitem.headline: Waigel says reforms to cut net tax burden.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Monday that the next tax burden on Germans should fall by between 20 and 30 billion marks in a major tax reform he wants to implement in 1999.
Waigel, speaking at a tax forum of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), also said that tax authorities should do more to determine taxable trading gains.
Waigel said the top rate of German income tax should be cut to below 40 percent from 53 percent now, but added he wanted to keep some room for manoeuvre in setting levels.
"Thirty-five to 40 percent is a range within which we will become internationally competitive," Waigel said. He also said the entry tax rate should fall from just under 26 percent now.

Germany's Sunday papers carried reports of a tax plan penned by Kohl's parliamentary lieutenant Wolfgang Schaueble foreseeing a cut in the top tax rate to 35 percent from 1999 and an entry rate of under 20 percent.

Waigel was said to have approved the document, which will be put to the CDU leadership for approval before going to the annual party conference on October 22. Waigel told delegates gross tax cuts of between 80 and 90 billion marks would come on top of already planned reductions in corporation and withholding taxes and Germany's solidarity surcharge. But, he added, some tax breaks would have to go.
